newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto says three parties enough.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto says three parties enough.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto has dimissed calls to allow more political parties to contest the country's general elections, the Jakarta Post newspaper reported on Saturday.
"It would be impossible to add another party," Suharto told university students in a meeting on Friday.

Indonesia allows only the ruling Golkar party, Moslem-orientated United Development Party (PPP) and Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Demoractic Party (PDI) to contest tightly-controlled general elections held every five years.
Suharto said the current system had evolved over 20 years in a long and painful process of consensus-building.

"Those who insist on a multiparty system similar to what they have abroad, or the one we had a long time ago, are automatically asking that we repeal the five political laws that we enacted by consensus. This will be a setback," he said.

"This is clearly unrealistic if we look at the history of this country in the last 20 years and at the way we have upheld the law and implemented the (state) Pancasila ideology and the 1945 Constitution," Suharto said.

The political laws limit the number of organisations which can contest the elections to three, regulate election campaigns and the number of seats in parliament and require that all social and political organisations adhere to Pancasila.
"This system has ensured six stable administrations, each one governing for five uninterrupted years," Suharto said.
"Why would anyone fail to see (the benefit) of this and want to revert back to the multiparty system or move to a liberal and irresponsible system?" he said.
Local government authorities closed the office of ousted PDI leader Megawati Sukarnoputri on Friday on the grounds that it violated zoning regulations.

The govenment no longer recognises Megawati as a party leader, despite an ongoing court case in which she is challenging her overthrow and the government support for a rebel congress in June which voted her out of office.
Witnesses said the office in East Jakarta was quiet with no sign of activity and no presence by security forces.

Megawati had tried to establish a new office after her supporters were expelled from PDI headquarters in central Jakarta by police on July 27 in an incident which sparked the city's worst riots in more than 20 years.
